title: Correlation matrix with significance: which parameters co-vary?
summary: A matrix of correlation coefficients between parameters, drawn as a colour grid on a diverging scale centred at zero, with the value printed in each cell. It shows which parameters move together and which are independent.

media.alt: A six by six colour matrix of correlation coefficients with a blue-white-red diverging colour bar from -1 to 1; red diagonal of ones, pale pink off-diagonal cells of 0.1 to 0.2, a block of 0.4 in the lower right among parameters 3, 4 and 5, and pale blue cells of -0.1 in the first row and column.
media.caption: Reference render of class F8.2 (design-system gallery). The data are synthetic and exist only to demonstrate the form.

source.note: Plot class from the design system's plot taxonomy; synthetic demonstration data.

read_the_figure.question: Which parameters co-vary?
read_the_figure.axes: Both axes: parameter index 0 to 5. Colour: Pearson correlation coefficient from -1 (blue) through 0 (white) to +1 (red), with a colour bar. The value of each cell is printed to one decimal.
look_at: Is the colour scale diverging and centred on zero, so that positive and negative are different hues?
Which off-diagonal cells are far from white? Those are the parameters that co-vary.
Are the values printed so that a pale cell of 0.1 can be told from 0.2?
Is the sample size stated and are significant cells marked?
as_drawn: Six parameters. The diagonal is 1.0. Parameters 3, 4 and 5 are mutually correlated at 0.4; parameter 0 is near zero with the others (0.0 to 0.1, and -0.1 with parameters 3 and 5); the other pairs are 0.1 to 0.2.
The diverging colour map runs from blue at -1 to red at +1 with white at 0; the colour bar is labelled in steps of 0.25.
Each cell prints its value to one decimal, so differences below 0.05 are invisible, and the matrix is symmetric so every number appears twice.
No marks for significance are drawn and the number of samples is not printed (the class code uses 80), although the class name promises significance.
read_the_figure.proves: A cell far from zero in a sample of known size shows that two parameters move together linearly in that sample. It does not show causation, nor non-linear dependence, nor a relationship that is the same outside the sample.
if_wrong: A sequential (not diverging) colour map: the sign cannot be read.
Values near plus or minus 0.1 treated as real without a sample size: with n = 80 they are within noise.
A strong correlation caused by one outlier: always look at the scatter plot of any pair that matters.
must_check: diverging cmap centred at 0: sign is the second most important thing in a correlation, so the colour map must make positive and negative different and put the neutral colour at zero.
values printed: colour shows the pattern but not the number, and a significance judgement needs the number.

terms.meaning: The covariance of two variables divided by the product of their standard deviations; a measure of linear association between -1 and 1.
A colour map with two hues meeting at a neutral centre, used for quantities with a meaningful zero.
Whether a correlation of this size could plausibly arise by chance in a sample of this size.
The map z = arctanh r, for which r has an approximately normal distribution with standard error 1 / sqrt(n - 3).
Looking at many pairs makes a spurious 'significant' value likely; the threshold must be tightened.

remember: r = cov / (s_x s_y) lies between -1 and 1; 0 means no linear relationship.
Significance: t = r sqrt((n - 2) / (1 - r^2)) with n - 2 degrees of freedom.
For n = 80, |r| above 0.22 is significant at 5 percent for a single pair.
With 15 pairs, a Bonferroni threshold raises that to 0.32.
Correlation is not causation and does not see curves.

understand.title: Marks and encodings
understand.text: Row and column positions index the parameters, so each square is one pair. Colour encodes the correlation: hue gives the sign and saturation the strength, with white at zero. The printed number is a redundant encoding that makes the values exact. The diagonal is always 1 and carries no information.

understand.title: Why this form answers the question
understand.text: Plain language: if two parameters always move together you cannot tell their effects apart, and if they are independent you can. A matrix of all pairs shows the whole pattern at once, and a block of strong cells is the group of parameters that move as a team. The diverging colours let you see at a glance which pairs push in opposite directions.

understand.title: How it misleads
understand.text: Correlation measures only linear association: a perfect parabola can have r = 0. With 80 samples a coefficient of 0.1 is noise, yet in a colour grid it looks like a real pale pink. Looking at 15 pairs and calling the strongest 'significant' invites false positives. The matrix is symmetric and wastes half the space, and the ordering of the parameters decides whether blocks appear. And the colour scale must be fixed at plus or minus 1, or a narrow range of values would be stretched into vivid colour.

understand.title: Alternatives
understand.text: A scatter-plot matrix shows the shape of every pair, including curves and outliers. Rank correlation (Spearman) is robust to monotone curvature. A hierarchical-clustering reordering exposes blocks. For parameter inference, the posterior corner plot (F8.8) shows correlations of the quantity of interest.

understand.title: A variant to create
understand.text: Show only the lower triangle, mark cells that pass the Bonferroni threshold with an asterisk, grey out the others, print n in the caption, and reorder the parameters by clustering.

steps.title: Pearson correlation
steps.note: Dimensionless, unchanged by a change of units, and symmetric in x and y.

steps.title: Is a correlation significant?
steps.note: For n = 80 and alpha = 0.05 this gives 0.22; for a Bonferroni level of 0.05 / 15 (15 pairs) it gives 0.32.

steps.title: An interval for r = 0.4
steps.note: With n = 80 a correlation of 0.4 is clearly positive but known only to within 0.2 to 0.57.

worked.title: Reading the correlation matrix of the reference render
worked.problem: (1) Which pairs of parameters are most strongly correlated? (2) If the sample size is 80, which of the printed values are distinguishable from zero? (3) What is a plausible range for the true correlation of parameters 3 and 4?

solution.text: (1) The red block of parameters 3, 4 and 5: all three pairs read 0.4.
(2) The threshold for a single pair is 0.22 and for fifteen pairs 0.32. Only the three 0.4 cells pass both; 0.2 values are borderline for a single pair, and values of 0.1 or less are within noise.

worked.answer: The block of parameters 3, 4 and 5 at 0.4 each; only these exceed the significance threshold; the true correlation of 3 and 4 is between about 0.2 and 0.57.

analyze.q: Why can two variables with an obvious relationship have a correlation close to zero?
analyze.hint: Think of y = x squared on a symmetric range.

analyze.q: The matrix is symmetric. How would you redraw it to use the space better?
analyze.hint: Lower triangle plus a second quantity in the upper triangle.

analyze.q: Why does a colour bar from -0.5 to 0.5 mislead?

evaluate.q: A report says parameters 3 and 4 are linked. What would you check before accepting it?
evaluate.hint: Scatter plot, sample size, outliers, other samples.

create: Redraw as a lower triangle with asterisks for pairs above the Bonferroni threshold and the sample size in the caption.
Add a scatter-plot matrix of parameters 3, 4 and 5 to check the shape of the relationship.

checks.q: Why use a diverging colour map for correlations?
checks.answer: Because zero is meaningful and the sign matters; two hues meeting at white make positive and negative visibly different and put no correlation in the neutral colour.

checks.q: n = 30 and r = 0.3. Compute the t statistic.
checks.answer: t = 0.3 x sqrt(28 / 0.91) = 0.3 x 5.55 = 1.66, below the critical value of about 2.05: not significant.

checks.q: You examine 45 pairs and find one with p = 0.03. What do you conclude?
checks.answer: With 45 tests about two false positives at the 0.05 level are expected by chance, so a single p of 0.03 is weak evidence; use a corrected threshold and check the result on new data.
